title: Elon Musk's Big Wireless Ambition: SpaceX Targets 80,000 Cell Sites to Launch Starlink Mobile
snippet: SpaceX is laying the groundwork for a fourth nationwide wireless carrier to challenge AT&T, Verizon, and T-Mobile, but analysts warn the price tag could reach tens of billions of dollars.
content:
Elon Musk is setting his sights on a new frontier: terrestrial cellular service. SpaceX is taking concrete steps to build out "Starlink Mobile," aiming to establish a fourth major nationwide wireless carrier alongside incumbents Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile.

Reports surfaced this week that SpaceX is in active negotiations with major telecommunications infrastructure operators, including Crown Castle, to access roughly 80,000 cell sites across the United States. The prospect of fresh competition rattled Wall Street, sending shares of AT&T and T-Mobile down as much as 6% on Friday, while Verizon slipped 1.5%.

A Massive Financial and Technical Mountain

To back up its cellular ambitions, SpaceX recently spent an estimated $8 billion to acquire a nationwide portfolio of low-band spectrum in the 800 MHz range. The company plans to merge these low-frequency licenses with its vast constellation of Starlink satellites and ground-based antennas, creating a hybrid connectivity network capable of broad geographic reach and deep indoor signal penetration.

However, industry analysts warn that matching the coverage and performance of established carriers carries a staggering price tag. Goldman Sachs estimates that leasing 80,000 cell sites could cost SpaceX upwards of $4 billion annually in tower rent alone—translating to $20 billion to $40 billion over standard multi-year leasing periods. That figure excludes the massive additional capital needed for specialized radios, backhaul infrastructure, and operational maintenance.

Incumbents Dig In for a Long Battle

Telecom executives remain skeptical that Starlink Mobile can pose an immediate threat. Speaking on an earnings call, AT&T CEO John Stankey noted that building scaled, high-performance mobile networks requires decades of continuous investment and infrastructure tuning to deliver the reliability consumers take for granted.

Despite the long timeline, established carriers aren't taking any chances. Verizon, AT&T, and T-Mobile, working through industry trade group CTIA, have stepped up lobbying efforts at the Federal Communications Commission. In recent filings, the lobby urged regulators to preserve strict spectrum rules and protect primary terrestrial licensees against emerging satellite-based entrants.

While matching traditional carriers in dense metropolitan markets will prove a daunting task, SpaceX's hybrid satellite-terrestrial approach signals a fundamental shift in how cellular coverage could be delivered in the years ahead.
